unit_label: BFM Module C unit 6 (courseware unit 24): derivative products

facts.statement: Derivatives and the treasury (courseware): treasury uses derivatives chiefly to manage risk (including ALM risk), to meet the requirements of clients (especially corporate customers) and to take a trading position. A derivative does not have an independent value: its value derives from an underlying market or exposure (a financial market such as foreign exchange, bonds and equities, a commodity market such as oil, gold, cotton and wheat, or an index; also events such as rainfall or weather). A derivative is a financial contract specifying an underlying price, rate or index, a notional amount and/or payment provisions with clear settlement terms; it always refers to a future price and its value depends on the spot market. Forward contracts for exchange rates are the conventional derivative of exporters and importers; rupee derivatives are of recent origin and some products are still regulated by the central bank.

OTC versus exchange traded derivatives (courseware): over-the-counter (OTC) products are structured by banks to suit the client risk appetite, size and maturity (for example a forward or option on USD for any date and amount) and are negotiated directly with banks and investment institutions (in India only authorised banks may offer them); exchange traded derivatives are standardised contracts for a specified sum and period traded on a futures exchange (currency, interest rate, commodity, stock and index futures and options). Differences: OTC contract date, amount and terms are as the client wants, while exchange contracts are standardised (for example a USD 1000 contract settling on the last Wednesday of a month in rupees); OTC price is the bank quote with a margin, exchange price is transparent through order matching; OTC security is cash margin or charge on assets at the bank discretion, the exchange collects daily margin (mark to market); OTC has counterparty risk (bank risk, remote) while the exchange is counterparty to all and manages risk through margining; OTC settlement is mostly by physical delivery (net settlement only for cancellations) while exchange contracts mostly settle net in cash; OTC is mostly used for hedging an underlying risk, exchange products for trading and speculation. Bank treasuries and corporates mostly use OTC forward contracts, options and swaps; larger banks (market makers) cover residual positions in futures. Where the futures exchange is active, OTC prices largely reflect exchange prices, though OTC volume is much larger. In India trading in currency and interest rate derivatives is restricted to authorised banks except in the futures market where individuals, corporates and other entities can participate (subject to restrictions on non-resident entities).

Forward contract (courseware): a forward contract is a contract to deliver foreign currency on a future date at a fixed exchange rate; it is an OTC product with a bank as the counterparty. Example: a 3-month forward sale at Rs 77.00 per dollar lets an exporter sell the contracted amount to the bank at 77.00 whatever the market rate at expiry, even if the rupee has appreciated to Rs 75; a forward purchase protects an importer against depreciation of the rupee. Delivery must be given or taken as per contract; otherwise the contract is cancelled and the difference between spot and the contract rate is credited or recovered. On request banks may allow delivery within a window known as an option forward (the bank quotes the forward premium or discount applicable to the start or end date of the option period, whichever is worse to the client). Forward rate: the interest rate differential of the two currencies; the currency with the higher interest rate is always at a forward discount, the other at a premium (domestic rupee interest is higher than dollar interest, so forward rupee is at a discount to the dollar, the forward dollar at a premium, and the USD/INR forward rate is higher than spot). For freely convertible currencies the premium or discount equals the difference in risk-free interest rates; for the rupee, which is not fully convertible, it is also affected by supply and demand for forward dollars. A forward contract fixes the rate and gives zero risk on the hedged amount, but the holder cannot benefit if the market rate is better on the date of utilisation: the disadvantage is opportunity cost.

Options: terms and moneyness (courseware): an option gives the buyer (holder) a right but no obligation to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying (currency, bond, commodity, equity) at a prefixed rate (strike price) on or before a specified date (expiry). American options can be exercised any time up to expiry; European options only on the expiry date (the courseware says India uses only European options). A currency option example: a dollar put/yen call for USD 1 million with a strike of 105 JPY per dollar: if at expiry the market is 108 the holder will not exercise (can get more yen in the market); if at expiry the market is 100, the holder exercises, since the strike is better than the market. Moneyness: at-the-money (ATM) when the strike equals the spot (for a European option, the forward rate for the expiry); in-the-money (ITM) when the strike is better than the market (a call is ITM if the strike is below the forward rate, a put if the strike is above it); out-of-the-money (OTM) when the strike is worse. Premium is the price paid upfront by the buyer to the seller; it has two components: intrinsic value (call: spot minus strike, put: strike minus spot, never below zero; ATM and OTM options have none) and time value (the premium less intrinsic value; maximum for an ATM option; it declines as the option becomes more ITM or OTM and as expiry approaches). Premium depends on volatility, time to expiry, interest rates and the strike; it rises with volatility, maturity and intrinsic value.

Option features and uses (courseware): the buyer can exercise whatever the market price at expiry, so profit potential is unlimited; the seller (writer) is obliged to buy or sell at the strike so the potential loss is unlimited; option positions are on a notional amount with only the difference exchanged, so little investment is needed (high leverage); the buyer pays the premium upfront. A currency option always has two legs: a put on USD against JPY at strike X is also a call on JPY. Options on bonds (price linked to interest rates) and equity (for example a put on shares at a strike gives the holder the right to sell at that strike; index options protect against a fall in an index) work the same way. Options are mainly used as a hedge, like insurance against adverse price movements: an exporter wants the rupee to depreciate, so a USD put option protects against appreciation; an importer wants the rupee to appreciate, so a USD call option protects; banks as intermediaries sell the option to the client and cover by buying the opposite option. A plain vanilla option has no conditionality; combinations (structured options such as zero-cost structures and range forwards, where the holder gives up some benefit to reduce premium, and barrier options) are riskier, often called exotics, and are generally not suitable for hedging market risk.

Option versus forward (courseware): a forward must be executed at the contracted rate on expiry, whereas the option holder may choose to exercise or not and may deal at the strike or the market rate, whichever is better; the forward rate is fixed at the current market quote and no fee is payable (the quote includes the bank margin), whereas the option premium is payable at the start and depends on volatility, interest rates and other factors; the forward premium is the interest differential of the two currencies, while the option premium is set by several factors; a forward is a simple contract while options range from plain vanilla to complex structures; for forwards both parties have only counterparty risk (no market risk once hedged), for options the buyer has full upside benefit and a limited loss (the premium) while the writer has unlimited risk. Options are also used in structuring credit products: a bond with a put option lets the investor sell it back to the issuer before maturity; a call option lets the issuer prepay; perpetual debt instruments of banks may carry a call option; a convertible option lets a bondholder convert debt to equity. Such inbuilt options are called embedded options and affect the pricing of the bond.

Futures (courseware): a futures contract is a forward contract traded on a futures exchange: the seller agrees to deliver to the buyer a specified security, currency or commodity on a specified date at a fixed price. Financial futures (currency, interest rate or bond, equity or stock index) are distinct from commodity futures; contracts have standard size and prefixed settlement dates. Example: a futures contract on GBP 25,000 at USD 1.3700 for delivery on 28 March, with spot at 1.34; on the settlement date, if the market rate of GBP is 1.40, the seller pays the holder the difference between the contract price and the spot price (1.40 - 1.37 = USD 0.03 per pound, so USD 750) and the seller bears the loss; if the market is below 1.37, the buyer bears the loss. Three differences from forwards: the buyer and seller deal with the exchange (which guarantees performance), not with each other; the contract is marked to market daily, with losses recovered from the holder as margin and gains credited; and futures are actively traded on the exchange, bought and sold several times during the day. In India currency futures for USD/INR started in August 2008 (contract size USD 1000, settled in rupees); cross currency contracts followed (EUR, GBP, JPY pairs); settlement is in rupees. Hedgers must buy or sell whole contracts, so a hedge may not match the exposure exactly: the difference between the exposure and the contract face value is basis risk (for example an exposure of USD 560,700 needs 561 contracts of USD 1000, leaving a mismatch of USD 300).

Interest rate futures (courseware): interest rate futures are contracts on fixed income securities (treasury bills, bonds) of specified size; those on treasury bills have short-term rates and those on bonds medium and long-term rates. A futures contract on a treasury bill trades at a discount equal to the interest rate for the period; for example if the expected interest rate at the end of the period is 4 per cent, the futures price is 100 - 4 = 96. Prices fluctuate daily with the perception of rates for the residual maturity. They hedge interest rate risk on the inverse relation between interest rates and bond prices: if rates rise, bond prices fall; a corporate expecting to borrow after 3 months and wishing to lock in the current rate would sell (short) the 90-day treasury bill futures; if rates rise by the date of the loan, the futures price falls and the profit on the futures compensates for the higher interest cost on the loan. The Indian interest rate futures market was relaunched in August 2009 after a failed attempt in 2003 (contract size and underlying details not taught); the courseware says it was thinly traded.

Interest rate swaps (courseware): a swap is an exchange of cash flows. An interest rate swap (IRS) is an exchange of interest flows on an underlying asset or liability, calculated on a notional principal that is never exchanged; the actual payment is netted on each interest payment date. Types by change of basis: fixed to floating, floating to fixed or floating to floating (basis swap, different benchmarks). Illustration: a company paying a fixed 7 per cent on a 5-year debenture expects rates to fall and swaps with a bank: the bank pays the company 7 per cent fixed (neutralising the debenture interest) and the company pays the bank floating, say 3-month T-bill plus 2 per cent. If the T-bill is 4 per cent the company pays 6 per cent and receives 7 per cent, saving 1 per cent; if the T-bill rises above 5 per cent the net flow is negative and the company pays the difference. A company with a floating rate loan that expects rates to rise would pay fixed and receive floating. The payer of the fixed rate is the buyer of the swap and the receiver of the fixed rate is the seller. A benchmark rate is a risk free interest rate determined by the market and widely accepted, so that the interest paid reflects market trends; for USD benchmarks the alternate reference rate (SOFR, the secured overnight financing rate) replaced LIBOR; in India the most popular benchmark is the overnight MIBOR; others include G-sec yields, the 90-day T-bill and a commercial paper index (the courseware describes the constant maturity swap). A floating to floating (basis) swap lets a company move from, for example, T-bill to MIBOR-linked flows. Quanto and coupon swaps, swaptions and swaps with knock-out levels are exotic; in the rupee market the courseware says only plain vanilla swaps are permitted. The type of swap depends on the client needs; treasury also uses swaps to bridge asset-liability mismatches and hedges its residual position through swaps and futures.

Swap counterparty risk and forward rate agreements (courseware): the counterparty risk on an IRS is limited to the net interest payable by one counterparty to the other, depending on whether the floating or the fixed rate is higher at each reset, so credit conversion factors are applied to the notional principal to reckon capital charge (the factors rise with tenor and are higher for exchange rate contracts; the table is not taught). A forward rate agreement (FRA) is closely linked to an IRS but covers a single payment in the future whereas an IRS covers a series of payments. Example: a loan whose interest rate is due to be reset on 29 June runs a risk that the reference rate may be much higher than today: a 6/12 FRA fixes the interest rate 6 months hence for the next 6-month period (ending 12 months from now); the floating reference rate is decided in advance (one day before the period), but interest is paid at the end; the FRA settlement takes place at the beginning of the period and is discounted for the period, so the effective rate is the same. Swap valuation uses the risk-free yield curve (G-sec in India) by interpolation; as the swap market becomes liquid, swap curves based on traded rates are used.

Currency swaps (courseware): a currency swap is an exchange of cash flows in one currency for those in another (principal and/or interest under a loan). Variants: a principal only swap (POS) hedges only the currency (the borrower continues to pay interest in USD and uses the principal in domestic currency, repaying at a fixed rate of exchange, so no exchange risk); a coupon only swap (COS) hedges only the interest rate (the USD loan is used in the same currency but interest on the USD loan is swapped into rupee interest; principal repayment is as per the original terms, and if not otherwise hedged, an appreciating rupee reduces the rupee cost of repaying); a principal plus interest swap (P+I) removes both currency risk and interest rate risk, with principal and interest paid in domestic currency. The need arises from a currency mismatch (for example a lender wants to lend in a currency different from the one in which the borrower earns revenue), and complementary needs of two parties can be matched by a bank intermediary. Indian companies that raise ECB in USD, euro or yen often swap the loan into rupees, but the effective cost is not much lower than a rupee loan since there is no arbitrage between major currencies: the swap cost represents the interest rate differential (forward exchange contracts) and interest rate forwards; net benefit arises only from a difference in credit spread over the risk free rate. The currency swap combines forward currency rates and interest rate swap rates for the relevant period. Illustration: a USD 100 million loan at 6-month LIBOR plus 200 basis points with bullet repayment after 5 years, swapped with a bank at INR 4,400 million with fixed 6.50 per cent a year on the rupee principal, the customer paying fixed rupee interest and receiving 6m L + 200 bps on USD 100 million and re-exchanging principal at the end.

Developments in Indian markets and documentation (courseware, concept only): until 1998 forward contracts were the only derivative; IRS and FRA were allowed in 1999 (plain vanilla only for banks); corporates may use IRS only for hedging; banks, primary dealers and financial institutions may use IRS for hedging, balance sheet management and market making; banks may trade for market making; rupee USD options were allowed from June 2003 for hedging of underlying transactions; exchange traded currency options were permitted later with prudential eligibility requirements (stated in the courseware, not taught); inter-bank OTC derivative trades are reported to the clearing corporation. Documentation: all derivative contracts are bound by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) standards in three stages: the ISDA Master Agreement (jurisdiction, valuation norms, credit enhancement, cross-default; executed once covering all transactions between two parties), the Schedule (customisation) and the Trade Confirmation for each trade; the confirmation prevails over the schedule and the schedule over the master agreement. Derivative guidelines of 2007 and 2011 after structured product losses in 2005-08: derivatives may be offered only to corporates with a risk management policy approved by the board, and banks must have a suitability and appropriateness policy to avoid mis-selling; trading positions in forwards, options and IRS must be marked to market daily; derivatives are subject to board-approved internal policy. Interest rate options (European calls, puts, caps, floors and collars) were introduced from January 2017 for balance sheet management and market making. Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd (FBIL), formed by the market bodies (FIMMDA, FEDAI and IBA), administers benchmarks (overnight MIBOR, term MIBOR, MIFOR, volatility matrices, certificates of deposit and treasury bill rates) free of the conflicts of interest of earlier arrangements; MIFOR combines the USD reference rate and the forward premium of USD/INR. Details, dates and conditions are not taught.

payload.title: What derivatives are and how treasury uses them
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **derivative** has **no independent value**: its value **derives from an underlying** market or exposure: a **financial market** (currency, bonds, equities), a **commodity** (oil, gold, cotton, wheat), an **index**, or even an event such as **rainfall**.

It is a **financial contract** with an underlying price, rate or index, a **notional amount** and/or payment terms, and **clear settlement terms**. It always refers to a **future price**, and its value **depends on the spot market**.

**Treasury uses derivatives to:** **manage risk (including ALM risk)**, **serve clients** (especially corporates) and **take trading positions**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The notional amount sets the scale of payments; it need not be exchanged.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a derivative said to have no independent value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its value is derived from an underlying market or exposure.

payload.title: OTC versus exchange traded derivatives
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Feature | **OTC** | **Exchange traded** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Terms** | **Tailored** date, amount and terms | **Standardised** size and settlement dates |
| **Price** | **Bank quote plus margin** | **Transparent**, order matching |
| **Security** | **Cash margin or charge** at the bank discretion | **Daily margin**, marked to market |
| **Counterparty risk** | **Bank risk** (remote) | The **exchange is counterparty** and manages risk |
| **Settlement** | Mostly **physical delivery** | Mostly **net cash settlement** |
| **Use** | Mostly **hedging** | **Trading and speculation** |

Bank treasuries and corporates mostly use **OTC forwards, options and swaps**; **market-making banks** cover residual positions in **futures**. In India, currency and interest rate derivatives in the OTC market are restricted to **authorised banks**, while **individuals and corporates** can use **futures** (restrictions apply to non-residents).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: OTC volume is larger, but exchange prices often guide OTC quotes.

self_check.prompt_text: Who is the counterparty to every trade on a futures exchange?

payload.title: Forward contract and forward premium
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **forward contract** delivers foreign currency on a **future date** at a **fixed rate**; it is **OTC** with a **bank** as counterparty.

- **Exporter:** a 3-month forward sale at **Rs 77.00** locks 77.00 **even if the rupee appreciates to 75**.
- **Importer:** a forward purchase protects against **rupee depreciation**.
- **Delivery** must be given or taken; if not, the contract is **cancelled** and the **difference to spot** is credited or recovered.
- **Option forward:** delivery allowed within a **window**; the bank quotes the **worse** of the start or end premium for the client.

**Forward rate:** from the **interest rate differential**. The currency with the **higher** interest rate is at a **forward discount**; the other at a **premium**. Rupee interest is above dollar interest, so the **forward dollar is at a premium** (higher than spot). For free currencies the premium **equals the risk-free interest difference**; for the rupee, **supply and demand for forward dollars** also matter.

**Disadvantage:** **opportunity cost** if the market rate is better on the date of use.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A forward removes risk and opportunity alike.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency trades at a forward discount?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The one with the higher interest rate.

payload.title: Forward rate from interest differential (simple form)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forward rate = Spot x (1 + r_quote x n/365) / (1 + r_base x n/365).**

**Forward premium (annualised, per cent) = (Forward - Spot) / Spot x 365 / n x 100.**

**Cost of a forward cover = (Forward - Spot) per unit of foreign currency.**

**Effective rate for an exporter selling forward = forward rate** (no gain from a better market rate).

**Opportunity cost = (market rate at expiry - contracted rate) per unit**, when the market is better.

formula_spec.latex_expression: F = S \times \frac{1 + r_q n/365}{1 + r_b n/365}

variables.name: Interest rate of the quoted currency
Interest rate of the base currency

payload.expanded_explanation_md: For the rupee the actual forward can differ because of forward supply and demand.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the opportunity cost of a forward sale at 77 if the market at expiry is 79?

payload.title: Options: terms, moneyness and premium
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **option** gives the buyer a **right but no obligation** to **buy (call)** or **sell (put)** an underlying at a **strike price** on or before **expiry**. **American** options can be exercised **any time to expiry**; **European** only **on expiry** (the courseware says India uses European options).

**Example:** a **dollar put / yen call**, USD 1 million, strike **105**: market **108** at expiry: **not exercised**; market **100**: **exercised** (strike better than market).

| Moneyness | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ITM** | **Strike better than market** (call: strike below forward; put: strike above) |
| **ATM** | Strike **equals** spot (forward for a European option) |
| **OTM** | Strike **worse** than market |

**Premium** (paid upfront) = **intrinsic value + time value**.

- **Call intrinsic = spot - strike**; **put intrinsic = strike - spot**; **never below zero**.
- **Time value** is **greatest at the money** and **shrinks as expiry nears** or the option goes deeper ITM or OTM.
- Premium **rises** with **volatility**, **maturity** and **intrinsic value**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: An option that is OTM has only time value.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the two parts of an option premium?

payload.title: Option payoff and profit
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Call payoff at expiry = max(S - K, 0).** **Put payoff = max(K - S, 0).**

**Buyer profit = payoff - premium.** **Writer profit = premium - payoff.**

**Break-even:** call **K + premium**; put **K - premium**.

**Time value = premium - intrinsic value.**

Buyer maximum loss = **premium**; writer maximum gain = **premium**.

common_errors: Using the wrong sign for a put

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The buyer loss is limited to the premium; the writer loss can be large.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the buyer maximum loss on an option?

payload.title: Option features and use as a hedge
payload.core_explanation_md:
- The buyer's **profit potential is large** (unlimited for a call) and the loss limited to the **premium**; the **writer** is obliged to perform at the strike, so the writer **can lose heavily**.
- Options are on a **notional** amount, so **little investment** is needed: **high leverage**.
- A currency option has **two legs**: a **put on USD against JPY** is also a **call on JPY**.
- Options exist on **bonds**, **equities** and **indices** (a put on shares or an index protects against a fall).

**Hedging:** like **insurance**. An **exporter** (wants the rupee weak) buys a **USD put**; an **importer** (wants the rupee strong) buys a **USD call**. A bank sells the option to the client and **covers by buying the opposite option**.

**Structures:** **plain vanilla** options are simple. **Zero-cost structures, range forwards and barrier options** give up some benefit to cut the premium; they are **riskier**, often called **exotics**, and **not suited** to hedging market risk.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Giving up upside to lower the premium transfers risk back to the buyer.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency option protects an importer?

payload.title: Option versus forward, and embedded options
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **Forward** | **Option** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execution** | **Must be executed** at the contracted rate | Holder **may choose** to exercise or deal in the market |
| **Cost** | **No fee**; quote includes bank margin | **Premium paid upfront** |
| **Pricing** | **Interest differential** | **Volatility, rates, strike, time** |
| **Structure** | Simple | Plain vanilla to complex |
| **Risk** | Locked: **no gain or loss** vs. the hedged amount | Buyer: **full upside, loss limited to premium**; writer: **large risk** |

**Embedded options** inside bonds: a **put** (investor sells back before maturity), a **call** (issuer prepays), a **convertible** option (debt to equity); they affect **bond pricing**. Banks' perpetual debt instruments may carry a call option.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The premium is the price of keeping the favourable side of the market.

self_check.expected_takeaway: An option built into a product such as a bond, for example a put, call or conversion right.

payload.title: Futures and how they differ from forwards
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **futures contract** is a **forward traded on an exchange**: the seller agrees to deliver a **specified security, currency or commodity** on a **set date** at a **fixed price**; size and dates are **standard**.

**Example:** GBP 25,000 at USD 1.3700; at expiry the market is **1.40**: the seller pays **(1.40 - 1.37) = USD 0.03 per pound x 25,000 = USD 750**; if the market is below 1.37 the **buyer** bears the loss.

**Three differences from forwards:**

1. Parties deal with the **exchange**, which **guarantees performance**.
2. **Daily mark to market**: losses are recovered as **margin**, gains credited.
3. Futures are **actively traded** and can be bought and sold many times a day.

**India:** **USD/INR currency futures from August 2008** (USD 1000 per contract, **settled in rupees**); cross-currency contracts followed.

**Basis risk:** hedgers must use **whole contracts**: exposure **USD 560,700** needs **561 contracts of USD 1000**: mismatch **USD 300**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Standard contract sizes mean the hedge is rarely exact.

self_check.prompt_text: What is basis risk in a futures hedge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The mismatch between the exposure and the face value of the whole contracts used to hedge it.

payload.title: Futures hedge: contracts, mark to market and basis mismatch
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Contracts needed = exposure / contract size** (round to a whole number).

**Mismatch (basis) = contracts x size - exposure.**

**Futures gain or loss (long) = (settlement price - contract price) x contract size x contracts.**

**Daily mark to market = (today settlement - yesterday settlement) x size x contracts.**

assumptions: Positions held to the mark date
common_errors: Using the wrong side (short loses when price rises)

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A short position gains when the futures price falls.

self_check.prompt_text: How many USD 1,000 contracts hedge an exposure of USD 245,600?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 246 contracts (rounded to the nearest whole contract).

payload.title: Interest rate futures
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate futures** are contracts on **fixed income securities**: **T-bill futures** for short rates; **bond futures** for medium and long rates.

- A T-bill futures price is quoted at a **discount equal to the interest rate**: expected rate **4 per cent** gives a futures price of **100 - 4 = 96**.
- **Rates up, prices down**.
- **Hedge:** a corporate that will **borrow in 3 months** and wants to lock in today's rate **sells (shorts) 90-day T-bill futures**; if rates rise, the **futures price falls** and the **gain on the futures offsets the higher loan interest**.
- The Indian market was **relaunched in August 2009** after a failed 2003 attempt, and was thin (courseware).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Selling futures profits when rates rise, which offsets the higher borrowing cost.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the futures price when the expected interest rate is 6 per cent?

payload.title: Interest rate swaps
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **interest rate swap (IRS)** exchanges **interest payments** on a **notional principal** that is **never exchanged**; only the **net** is paid on each date.

**Types:** **fixed to floating**, **floating to fixed**, **floating to floating (basis swap)**.

**Example:** a company pays **7 per cent fixed** on a 5-year debenture and expects rates to fall. It swaps: the **bank pays 7 per cent fixed** to cover the debenture and the **company pays floating (T-bill + 2 per cent)**. With T-bill at **4 per cent** the company pays **6** and receives **7**: **saving 1 per cent**. If the T-bill rises above 5 per cent, the company **pays the difference**.

A company with a **floating loan** that expects rates to rise **pays fixed, receives floating**. **Payer of fixed = buyer of the swap**; **receiver of fixed = seller**.

**Benchmark:** a **market-determined risk-free rate** (SOFR replaced LIBOR for USD; **overnight MIBOR**, G-sec yields, the 90-day T-bill and a CP index in India). **Exotics** (quanto, coupon swaps, swaptions, knock-out swaps) are not for ordinary use; only **plain vanilla swaps** are permitted in rupees (courseware).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Only the net amount moves, so credit exposure is far below the notional.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the notional principal exchanged in an interest rate swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, it is only used to calculate the interest payments.

payload.title: Net swap payment and saving
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Net payment (payer of fixed, receiver of floating) = (floating - fixed) x notional x days/365**; positive means the payer **receives**.

**Company saving in the example = fixed received - floating paid = 7% - (T-bill + 2%)** when the company is **paying** floating and **receiving** the fixed to offset its debenture.

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, fixed **7**, T-bill **4**: floating = **6**; saving **1 per cent** = **Rs 1 crore a year**.

common_errors: Reversing the direction of the net payment

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Read the direction of the payment from the point of view of the payer of fixed.

self_check.prompt_text: Who receives the net payment when the floating rate is above the fixed rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The party that pays fixed and receives floating.

payload.title: Swap counterparty risk and forward rate agreements
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Counterparty risk** on an IRS is limited to the **net interest** one side owes the other, depending on whether floating or fixed is higher at each reset. So **credit conversion factors** applied to the **notional** give the **capital charge** (factors rise with **tenor** and are higher for **exchange rate** contracts; table not taught).

**FRA (forward rate agreement):** like an IRS but for **one future payment**. A **6/12 FRA** fixes the rate for the **6-month period starting 6 months ahead**. The reference rate is set **in advance**, interest paid at the **end**, but the FRA is **settled at the start** of the period and **discounted**, so the effective rate is the same.

**Valuation:** swaps are valued on the **risk-free yield curve** (G-sec curve in India) by **interpolation**; traded swap curves are used as the market deepens.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Discounting the settlement removes the benefit of receiving it early.

payload.title: FRA settlement amount
payload.core_explanation_md:
For a **buyer** of an FRA (protects against rising rates):

**Settlement = Notional x (reference rate - FRA rate) x (d / 365) / (1 + reference rate x d / 365)**, paid at the **start** of the period.

A **positive** value is **received by the buyer**; a negative value is **paid**.

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, FRA rate **7 per cent**, reference **8 per cent**, **182 days**: settlement = 100 x 0.01 x 182/365 / (1 + 0.08 x 182/365) = **Rs 0.480 crore** (0.4795 rounded).

assumptions: Settlement at the start of the period
common_errors: Using the contract rate in the denominator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The denominator discounts an interest amount that would otherwise be paid at the end.

self_check.prompt_text: Who receives the FRA settlement when the reference rate exceeds the FRA rate?

payload.title: Currency swaps: POS, COS and principal-plus-interest
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **currency swap** exchanges cash flows in **one currency** for another (principal and/or interest).

| Variant | What is hedged |
| --- | --- |
| **Principal only swap (POS)** | **Currency risk**: interest stays in USD; principal in domestic currency at a **fixed exchange rate** |
| **Coupon only swap (COS)** | **Interest rate** (and currency of interest): USD interest swapped to **rupee interest**; principal repaid **as originally agreed** (currency risk on principal remains unless hedged otherwise) |
| **Principal plus interest (P+I)** | **Both** currency and interest rate risk removed |

**Why:** a **currency mismatch** between where funds can be raised cheaply and where revenue arises; a **bank intermediary** can match the needs.

**Cost reality:** Indian companies swap USD, euro or yen **ECB into rupees**, but the **effective cost is not much below a rupee loan**: between major currencies there is **no arbitrage**; the swap cost reflects the **interest differential** (forward rates and interest forwards). **Gain arises only from a difference in credit spread** over the risk-free rate.

A currency swap = **forward currency rates + interest rate swap rates** for the period.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A P+I swap turns a foreign currency loan into a fully domestic currency loan.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency swap removes both currency and interest rate risk?

payload.title: Currency swap cash flows
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Initial exchange:** principal swapped at the **spot rate**: **INR principal = USD principal x spot**.

**Periodic interest (customer pays):** **INR interest = INR principal x fixed rate x days/365 (or half-year)**; receives **USD interest = USD principal x (USD rate)**.

**Final exchange:** INR principal back, USD principal returned, at the **same initial rate**.

Example: **USD 100 million** at spot **44 per USD**: INR **4,400 million**; fixed **6.50 per cent** a year: half-year INR interest **= 4,400 x 0.065 / 2 = INR 143 million**.

assumptions: Principal exchanged at the initial rate at the start and end
common_errors: Using a half-year rate as annual

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because the final exchange uses the initial rate, exchange rate risk on principal is removed.

self_check.prompt_text: At what rate is principal re-exchanged at the end of a currency swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The same initial exchange rate fixed at the start.

payload.title: Documentation and the regulatory approach to derivatives
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ISDA documentation:** three layers.

1. **Master Agreement** (jurisdiction, valuation norms, credit enhancement, cross-default): signed **once** for all deals between two parties.
2. **Schedule** (customisation).
3. **Trade Confirmation** for each deal.

The **confirmation overrides the schedule**, and the **schedule overrides the master agreement**.

**Regulatory approach (concepts):**

- Plain vanilla IRS and FRA for banks; **corporates use IRS only for hedging**; banks may also use them for **balance sheet management and market making**.
- After heavy losses on **structured products in 2005-08**, derivatives may be offered only to **corporates with a board-approved risk management policy**, and banks need a **suitability and appropriateness policy** to avoid **mis-selling**.
- Trading and hedging positions must be **marked to market daily**.
- Inter-bank OTC derivative trades are **reported to the clearing corporation**.
- **Interest rate options** (European calls, puts, caps, floors, collars) were later introduced.
- **FBIL**, owned by the market bodies, administers benchmarks (**overnight MIBOR, MIFOR** and others) independent of conflicts of interest; **MIFOR** combines the USD reference rate with the **USD/INR forward premium**.

Dates, conditions and limits are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The hierarchy lets the specific trade terms override the general ones.

The courseware states that American options are prohibited after the 2008-09 crisis and that only European options are used in India; this is a courseware statement not verified and is taught only as the distinction between the two styles.
The courseware states that quanto swaps are now prohibited in India and that only plain vanilla swaps are permitted; taught as a courseware statement at its date, not as current rule.

The courseware worked examples were recomputed and agree: the 3-month forward sale at Rs 77.00 against a later spot of Rs 75; the GBP future (1.40 less 1.37 = USD 0.03 per pound on GBP 25,000 = USD 750); the 96 price of a futures contract at an expected rate of 4 per cent; the basis risk example (hedge USD 560,700 with 561 contracts of USD 1,000 leaves USD 300); the interest rate swap saving of 1 per cent (company pays T-bill plus 2 per cent against 7 per cent received).

The courseware discussion of options contains a loose passage (the option writer has "no market risk in plain vanilla option" and the buyer "has no risk"); the buyer has no risk beyond the premium and the writer does bear market risk; these statements are not taught as written. The option-versus-forward table is taught with that correction.
The courseware wording that a put on 1000 shares at a strike of Rs 9,000 trading at Rs 9,000 means the holder "can still sell" at 9,000 is taught as a put payoff illustration using invented numbers.
The courseware terminal questions were not copied; questions are independently written.
Numbers in the numerical items are invented and checked in tests/content/batch-bfm-c-u06-b001.test.ts.
